summary:
Microsoft polling of 5,000 UK employees and 1,000 senior business decision-makers finds a sharp confidence gap between leaders and workers on artificial intelligence. Released to coincide with Microsoft's Frontier Tour in London, the research reports that 84 percent of business leaders think Britain can become a world-leading AI economy within five years, against just 41 percent of employees. Nine in ten leaders say their organisation has a clear AI strategy, and 84 percent of those in adopting organisations say AI has brought moderate or significant changes to working practices, with 36 percent describing the changes as significant.

Employee attitudes are mixed rather than uniformly negative. Among workers already using AI, 71 percent say it has had a positive impact on their work or career and 69 percent say it has improved work quality. Yet 35 percent worry it has reduced their own job security and 57 percent fear it will shrink opportunities for young people and new entrants. Ninety percent of leaders expect AI to benefit British society over five years, compared with 49 percent of employees.

Both groups want more government action: 58 percent of employees and 62 percent of leaders. Priorities diverge, with employees favouring stronger regulation and safeguards (36 percent) and leaders favouring skills and training (35 percent) and business adoption support (30 percent).

Darren Hardman, CEO of Microsoft UK and Ireland, frames G7-leading adoption as a shared responsibility requiring work on skills and trust. An accompanying UK AI Diffusion Report estimates generative AI adoption rising from 36.6 percent in the first half of 2025 to 43.7 percent in the second quarter of 2026, ranking the UK eighth globally and second in the G7, with regional spread from 57.4 percent in the West of England Combined Authority to 34.1 percent in the Highlands and Islands. Microsoft promotes 'Frontier Firms' where staff work alongside AI agents, and cites a $30 billion UK investment commitment for 2025 to 2028.
